title: Praying behind another
hookLine: Muslims of different schools pray behind one another

lines: A STRANGE CITY, A STRANGE MOSQUE.
cards: A traveler steps off a bus in a city she has never seen, bag still on her shoulder, and follows the sound of the call to the nearest mosque. The prayer has already started.
She doesn't know the imam's name, which school his teachers followed, or how he was taught to wash before he stood up there.
She slips into the end of the last row, closes the gap beside a stranger, and raises her hands with everyone else. Should she have asked first? Does her prayer depend on details she can't see?

teach.b: The jurists asked it plainly. If the imam follows one school and I follow another, does my prayer behind him count? They argued over whose rules decide it, the imam's school or the follower's.
Some judged that if the imam's prayer is sound by his own school, the people behind him may follow him. Others added conditions. But the row kept forming.

teach.h: IF HE ERRS, IT IS AGAINST HIM.
teach.b: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said of those who lead the prayer, in meaning, they lead you, and if they get it right, it's for you and for them, and if they get it wrong, it's for you and against them.
The follower's prayer isn't hostage to every detail of the imam's. Then a story told in later books about Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. In his view, bleeding called for a fresh wudu.
Someone asked whether he would pray behind an imam who had bled and not washed again, following a school that didn't require it.

teach.h: HOW COULD I NOT PRAY BEHIND MALIK?
teach.b: The answer, as the story goes: how could I not pray behind Malik, or Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib? Great scholars, whose view on bleeding wasn't his. Last, the row itself.
In Bukhari, the Prophet tells the people to straighten their rows, and calls that part of establishing the prayer.

teach.h: SHOULDER TO SHOULDER, FOOT TO FOOT.
teach.b: Anas, a companion, describes them standing shoulder to shoulder, foot to foot. The row is built from bodies, not opinions: a Hanafi shoulder against a Shafi'i shoulder, the gap closed.
In Mecca, pilgrims from different schools pray behind the imams of the Sacred Mosque. The hands differ. The row doesn't.

how: In mosques with people from different schools, worshippers stand in one straight row behind one imam, each keeping their own school's details, such as where the hands are placed, while following the imam's movements.

o: joining a row led by an imam of a different school
praying alone at the back after the group has finished
standing in for an imam who is absent that day

s: the jurists never discussed praying behind an imam of another school
they argued over whose rules decide it, the imam's school or the follower's.
in the Bukhari report, the imam's mistake counts against him, not the follower
if they get it wrong, it's for you and against them.
the row is only straight if everyone holds their hands the same way
the row is shoulder to shoulder, foot to foot. hands can differ.

games.q: you're Imam Ahmad. you hold that bleeding calls for fresh wudu. the imam bled and didn't wash again, following a school that doesn't require it. do you pray behind him?
o: no: walk out and pray alone.
yes: how could I not pray behind such scholars?
pray, then repeat it at home.
games.why: as the story goes, he answered: how could I not pray behind Malik, or Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib? their view differed from his, and he still stood behind them.

practice: Sit or stand tall and feel your shoulders. Imagine a shoulder on either side touching yours, a stranger, a neighbor, someone whose way you don't share, and breathe with them. Don't fix their hands, and don't fix yours.

wordCard.voice: Praying behind another. Muslims of different schools stand in one row behind one imam, and the jurists worked out how each person's prayer still counts. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a row, a line of people standing together in prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: one row. Different hands, and still no gap. Rest well.
